items.title: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not zero
items.claim: Cool any substance and it gets denser as it approaches freezing — except water. Water reaches maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius and then becomes LESS dense as it cools further to 0 degrees Celsius.
items.prompt: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Trapped air bubbles make ice less dense than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice on freezing, so solid water occupies about 9 percent more volume than liquid water
Ice is colder, and colder things float
Surface tension on the underside of ice holds it up

items.reveal_title: Hydrogen bonding wins over packing efficiency
items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly, and molecules can crowd together. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral arrangement where each oxygen hydrogen-bonds to exactly four neighbours. That structure is open and roomy — about 9 percent more volume than the liquid.

This is why ponds freeze top-down rather than bottom-up. Fish survive winter because the densest water (4 degrees Celsius) sinks and the ice layer insulates everything below. If water behaved normally, lakes would freeze solid and life as we know it could not exist.
items.why: Students assume cooling always increases density. The hydrogen bond's geometry, not the temperature, controls the packing.

items.title: You can buy crystals of a 'noble gas' compound by the gram
items.claim: Xenon difluoride (XeF2) is sold by chemical suppliers. Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4) was first synthesised in 1962 by Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne National Lab. The textbook claim that noble gases 'do not react' was overturned 60 years ago.
items.prompt: What made xenon chemistry possible in 1962?

options.text: Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed xenon's first ionisation energy (1170 kJ/mol) is almost identical to O2's (1175 kJ/mol). Since PtF6 oxidised O2, he tried Xe + PtF6 — and got XePtF6, the first noble gas compound
Lasers were finally powerful enough to break Xe bonds

items.reveal:
In early 1962 Bartlett had been making PtF6 — a brilliant red solid — and noticed a sample turned red on contact with air. Analysis showed O2+ PtF6-: PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2.

Bartlett looked up xenon's first ionisation energy and saw the near-equality with O2. He reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise Xe. The synthesis of yellow XePtF6 made the front page of Chemical & Engineering News.

Within months Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating Xe and F2 in a nickel container at 400°C. Today there are dozens of xenon compounds (XeO3, XeO4, XeF6, KrF2, ArF — the last only at cryogenic temperatures).

Helium and neon remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — their ionisation energies (2080 and 2370 kJ/mol) are too high for any known oxidiser to defeat.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.

items.title: Some oxides react with BOTH acids and alkalis
items.claim: Sodium oxide reacts with acids only (it's basic). Sulfur trioxide reacts with alkalis only (acidic). But aluminium oxide and zinc oxide react with both — they are amphoteric.
items.prompt: What makes an oxide behave as both acid and base?

options.text: The element is metallic enough to lose electrons AND non-metallic enough to gain them
They are unstable and decompose in either

items.reveal:
Al2O3 + 6 HCl → 2 AlCl3 + 3 H2O (acts as base, accepting protons).
Al2O3 + 2 NaOH + 3 H2O → 2 Na[Al(OH)4] (acts as acid, accepting OH-).

Elements whose oxides are amphoteric sit near the diagonal that separates metals from non-metals on the periodic table — Be, Al, Ga, Ge, Sn, Pb, Sb. Their bonds with oxygen are intermediate in character: not fully ionic (like Na-O), not fully covalent (like S-O).

The Bayer process for extracting aluminium from bauxite uses amphoteric chemistry directly: hot NaOH dissolves Al2O3 from a mixture with iron oxide and silica; iron oxide doesn't dissolve and is filtered off.
items.why: Acid-base behaviour is taught as a binary classification. The boundary is fuzzy — and the fuzzy region is industrially crucial.
